Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

papers.title: The Kazdan-Warner equation on a finite graph with a Neumann boundary condition
papers.abstract:
We study the Kazdan-Warner equation $\Delta u = c - h \mathrm{e}^u$ on a finite connected domain $\Omega$ of a locally finite graph, with Neumann boundary data $\partial u / \partial
u = g$. We reduce the boundary condition to homogeneous form and use variational methods and upper and lower solutions to study solvability. Let $c_g \mathrel{:=} |\Omega|^{-1}\int_{\partial\Omega} g\, \mathrm{d}\mu$, and let $\psi$ solve $\Delta\psi = c_g$ with boundary data $\partial\psi / \partial
u = g$ and zero mean on $\Omega$. When $c = c_g$ and $h 
ot\equiv 0$, a solution exists if and only if $h$ changes sign and $\int_\Omega h \mathrm{e}^\psi\, \mathrm{d}\mu < 0$. When $c > c_g$, a solution exists if and only if $h$ is positive somewhere in $\Omega$. When $c < c_g$, solvability requires $\int_\Omega h \mathrm{e}^\psi\, \mathrm{d}\mu < 0$. Under this condition there is a threshold $-\infty \le c_-(h) < c_g$ such that a solution exists for $c_-(h) < c < c_g$ and no solution exists for $c < c_-(h)$. If $h \le 0$ and $h 
ot\equiv 0$, a solution exists for every $c < c_g$.

papers.title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
papers.abstract: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

papers.title: Circular decompositions for hyperbolic genus one knots
papers.abstract: We consider hyperbolic genus one knots having two or more non-isotopic, disjoint, genus one Seifert surfaces, with the property that the complementary regiones are handlebody pairs. We determine whether or not these knots have circular width equal to $(3)$. Moreover we give bounds on their circular widths. We also give explicit examples of such knots having three or five non-isotopic genus one Seifert surfaces and compute their circular widths. In particular this shows that many of these knots are non-almost fibered.

papers.title: Simultaneous spectral measurement and programmable filtering on a universal silicon photonic chip
papers.abstract: Spectral measurement and spectral filtering are two fundamental operations in optics, yet they are conventionally implemented using separate optical systems, hindering their simultaneous and programmable operation on a common platform. Here, we demonstrate a universal silicon photonic chip that unifies spectral measurement and programmable filtering within a single integrated architecture. The chip comprises two 8 * 8 programmable unitary transformation circuits interconnected through optical intensity modulators, forming a universal linear optical circuit. In contrast to conventional universal circuits employing equal-length interconnections, we deliberately introduce different optical path lengths between the two unitary circuits. The resulting wavelength-dependent phase evolution provides spectral diversity while preserving the programmability of the universal circuit, enabling parallel spectral measurement and programmable filtering. The fabricated chip achieves a spectral resolution of 0.05 nm over a bandwidth exceeding 100 nm, simultaneously measures eight independent laser sources, and generates multiple programmable spectral filter functions. We further demonstrate simultaneous spectral measurement and filtering during dynamic reconfiguration of the filter functions. These results establish universal photonic circuits as a versatile platform for integrating spectral sensing and programmable optical processing on a single chip.

papers.title: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
papers.abstract: Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

papers.title: Wei-Norman Factorization of Frenet-Serret equations and the Cardan Lock
papers.abstract: Frenet-Serret equations for particles moving along differentiable curves, in the case of non-constant curvature and torsion, are considered in the framework of the Wei-Norman factorization of the propagator using the Lie algebra of the rotation group. It leads to a system of coupled linear equations that are highly coupled if Euler or Cardan angles are used, but that can be uncoupled if the Cartan basis in the Lie algebra is used, resulting essentially in a Ricatti equation. However, since the rotations algebra is not a solvable algebra, the global Wei-Norman Theorem does not apply and singularities in the solutions of the system of equations appear at certain points, related to the \text{gimbal o Cardan lock}. Notwidthstanding, a detailed study of the limit at these points shows that in most of the cases the propagator is well defined and gimbal lock is avoided.

papers.title: Conditional limit theorems in dynamical systems
papers.abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive theory of conditional limit theorems for open dynamical systems. We study the statistical properties of the dynamics within transient regimes by establishing a suite of limit theorems describing the behavior of trajectories under the condition that they remain outside a ``hole'', or region of no return. Under a spectral gap assumption for the associated open transfer operator, we first establish conditioning and Yaglom limits and identify the corresponding conditionally invariant and conditionally ergodic measures. We then establish conditional exponential decay of correlations and the Strong Law of Large Numbers for both deterministic and quenched random systems. We also obtain a conditional Central Limit Theorem, Large Deviation Principle, and Berry--Esseen theorem, with additional assumptions in the quenched random case. We also derive standard (non-conditional) limit theorems on the surviving set of points that never enter the hole.

papers.title: From Persistent Cohomology to Maps into Arbitrary Eilenberg-MacLane Spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we address the construction of Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates (functions from datasets to Eilenberg-MacLane spaces $K(G,n)$) that encode nontrivial persistent cohomology classes in arbitrary dimensions $n$ and coefficient group $G$. The construction leverages the connecting homomorphism in the long exact sequence in Čech cohomology, from the short exact sequence of sheaves of continuous maps with values in $G$, $EG$ and $BG$. Crucially, the derivation is constructive: we give an explicit, recursive formula for preimages under the connecting homomorphism, which yields a constructive version of a classical cohomology vanishing theorem and, in turn, an algorithm for general Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates. We validate our approach through experiments on synthetic datasets, and present novel examples of $K(\mathbb{Z}/2, 2)$-coordinates not addressed in prior work.

papers.title: Gumbel Fluctuations of the Maximum of the Airy$_1$ Process
papers.abstract: We establish the Gumbel limit for the maximum of the Airy$_1$ process over $[0,N]$ as $N\to\infty$, with explicit centering of order $(\log N)^{2/3}$ and scale $(\log N)^{-1/3}$. The proof starts with a two-term expansion for the tail of the maximum over a fixed interval. Its leading term determines the centering, while the second term gives the joint-exceedance asymptotic for touching intervals. We then bound joint exceedances in separated unit intervals, uniformly over gaps up to a fixed multiple of the square root of the threshold. Covariance and mixing estimates control the larger gaps and complete the blocking argument.

papers.title: Theorems of the Alternative and Nonnegativity Certificates for Systems of Jensen-type Polynomials with Universal Quantifiers
papers.abstract: We introduce Jensen-type polynomials, a class of possibly nonconvex polynomials that extends the Jensen inequality for SOS-convex polynomials while retaining natural sums of squares (SOS) certificates for nonnegativity. We show that polynomials with essentially nonpositive coefficients belong to this class and establish a composition principle that yields further examples, including componentwise univariate compositions and compositions with structured quadratic maps motivated by source-localization loss functions. We then derive theorems of the alternative that provide SOS certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict inequalities involving Jensen-type polynomials and universally quantified variables. We illustrate our results through two applications, with numerical examples. First, we show that source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a simple dimension condition, and that an optimal solution can be recovered by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying the explicit Jensen map. Second, our SOS certificates yield two {\it convergent} SDP hierarchies for semi-infinite optimization with Jensen-type polynomials, providing upper and lower bounds on the optimal value. We also establish finite-convergence and solution-extraction results, under flat truncation rank condition and the associated Jensen maps.

papers.title: Radar-Native Control Barrier Functions: Doppler Range Rate as a Measured Barrier Derivative
papers.abstract: Safe control around dynamic obstacles requires information about both distance and relative motion. Range-based filters commonly reconstruct the required range rate from successive range measurements or from obstacle-state estimators, which can introduce estimator delay or sensitivity to range noise when obstacle motion changes. A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar measures radial relative velocity directly through Doppler. We use this measurement as the derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function (CBF) and obtain a closed-form filter on the robot's forward velocity. A measurement margin constructed from sensor error bounds accounts for errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing. In 508 paired encounters within the platform's retreat capability, direct Doppler produces two buffer incursions, compared with 15 for a constant-acceleration and 25 for a constant-velocity Kalman filter. On a Unitree Go1, the controller stops at $0.777 \pm 0.015$ m against the predicted $0.758$ m and reacts to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains. The guarantee covers the longitudinal range channel under bounded measurement errors and continuously available detections. Direct Doppler removes the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop, reducing the delay between a change in obstacle motion and its effect on the safety command.

papers.title: Faster polynomial-space algorithms for poset problems
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-space, deterministic, exact algorithm for counting linear extensions of partial orders over $n$ elements, with running time $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n}) \subseteq O(2.829^n)$. This improves upon the long-standing bound of $O^*(4^{n})$ attainable by standard divide and conquer (Savitch 1970, Gurevich and Shelah 1987). Our algorithm uses a similar balanced splitting approach as the classical algorithm, but applies it only to the elements outside a largest antichain. For the elements of the antichain itself we develop a formula based on inclusion-exclusion that accounts for the ways in which they can appear in a linear extension. The technique is also applicable to other problems on posets, which we illustrate by solving the well-studied jump number problem in a similar running time of $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n})$ and polynomial space. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with a running time below $4^n$ for both problems.

papers.title: A Dynamic Model and Stability Analysis of a Grid-Interactive Data Center
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of data centers is creating new interactions between computational workload and power-system dynamics, with potentially significant implications for grid stability. We develop a four-dimensional nonlinear dynamical model of a data center campus interconnected with the bulk power system through a modified Single Machine Infinite Bus system. The model couples generator swing dynamics with a fluid-limit model of computational workload backlog and a grid-interactive data center power controller that incorporates both frequency feedback and computational backpressure. This formulation captures the coupled evolution of generator frequency, rotor angle, computational workload, and data center power consumption, providing a framework for studying the stability implications of flexible data center operation.

papers.title: Convergence of the big J-function of a GKM manifold
papers.abstract: The genus-$0$ equivariant Gromov--Witten (GW) invariants of a GKM manifold can be computed recursively by a recursion discovered by Brown and studied further by Coates--Corti--Iritani--Tseng. In this paper, we prove a slightly modified version of this result by realizing the J-function as a solution to a fixed-point problem. As an application, we prove that both the equivariant and the non-equivariant quantum cohomologies of a GKM manifold are convergent. We also show that the equivariant central charges have no poles in the spectral parameter, compute their monodromy and their asymptotics at $z=0$, and formulate an equivariant mirror symmetry conjecture for GKM manifolds.

papers.title: Renormalization and exact Bloch bands: the trigonometric Rosen-Morse model
papers.abstract: We study the trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential as an isolated singular well and as an exactly solvable periodic lattice. The potential combines inverse-square singularities with Coulomb terms of opposite signs. In the strongly attractive regime, independent renormalization at the two endpoints gives a two-parameter family of spectra. Deep negative-energy levels form two asymptotic sequences with the same Efimov-like scaling and opposite first-order Coulomb corrections. In the weak-medium regime, self-adjoint matching conditions allow transmission between neighboring cells. We obtain the exact Bloch dispersion relation and determine the band widths, gaps, and electron and hole effective masses. At fixed band index, the bandwidth becomes exponentially small in the limit of large Coulomb coupling.

papers.title: Removable forests in $k$-connected and $k$-edge-connected graphs
papers.abstract: We prove the forest conjecture of Clay and Jordán: Let $k\ge1$ be an integer and let $F$ be a forest with $m$ vertices and $e$ edges. If a $k$-connected graph $G$ has minimum degree at least $\max\{k+e,m-1\}$, then it contains a copy of $F$ whose edge deletion preserves $k$-connectivity. We also prove the $k$-edge-connectivity version.

papers.title: Parisi Energy before Parisi Geometry in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
papers.abstract: The fractured low-energy landscape of spin glasses presents a notorious barrier to optimization. While high-depth calculations indicate that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can approach the Parisi ground-state energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, how it does so remains elusive. Here, we treat the QAOA distribution as a statistical-physics object and probe its geometry directly in the thermodynamic limit. We draw two independent bitstrings from the same problem instance and couple them through their macroscopic similarity. We find that typical QAOA samples remain macroscopically uncorrelated, even as their sensitivity to this coupling grows with circuit depth $p$. By contrast, the low-energy tail shows a much stronger tendency to overlap and reveals a Parisi-like phase with the same critical behavior as the thermal spin-glass transition. The onset of this organization moves toward the typical output as the circuit deepens, consistent with the separation vanishing only as $p\to\infty$. Together, these findings suggest a route distinct from structure-exploiting classical algorithms and thermal sampling, one in which the QAOA approaches the Parisi energy before Parisi geometry becomes typical.

papers.title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
papers.abstract: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

papers.title: A Tail-Geometric Approach to Kotlarski's Lemma with Order Statistics
papers.abstract: We develop a tail-geometric approach to nonparametric identification in repeated-measurement models based on large within-unit gaps. Differencing eliminates the common latent component, while conditioning on a large gap pushes the idiosyncratic errors into opposite tails. Under a regular thinner-than-Gaussian tail condition, an idiosyncratic component concentrates around a deterministic, gap-dependent location. Consequently, the corresponding observed measurement, after recentering, reveals the distribution of the common latent component up to location. The idiosyncratic distribution can then be recovered through deconvolution. This principle applies both to the classical two-measurement Kotlarski model and to settings where only order statistics are observed. Applications include auctions and wage-offer models, whether all offers are observed or only the top-ranked ones are available.

papers.title: Almost all vertex-transitive graphs and digraphs are Cayley
papers.abstract: We prove that almost all vertex-transitive digraphs are Cayley digraphs, and that almost all vertex-transitive graphs are Cayley graphs, as the number of vertices tends to infinity through all positive integers. The proportions of Cayley objects are at least $1-2^{-n/4+o(n)}$ for digraphs and $1-2^{-n/24+o(n)}$ for graphs. This proves the McKay--Praeger conjecture and its digraph analogue.

papers.title: Statistical robustness and time consistency in risk averse optimization
papers.abstract: The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.

papers.title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
papers.abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

papers.title: Redrock: Spectroscopic Classification and Redshift Fitting for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument
papers.abstract: Redrock is a software package for spectroscopic classification and redshift fitting, designed to use the full information from spectroperfectionism outputs: flux-calibrated spectra, uncorrelated errors, and a per-spectrum resolution matrix encoding the non-Gaussian wavelength-dependent spectral line-spread function. Redrock was originally developed for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), but the Extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS) also used Redrock as their primary galaxy redshift fitter prior to DESI. This paper presents the algorithmic details of Redrock and its performance on DESI data. On spectra from DESI DR2, Redrock achieves a redshift recovery rate of approximately 98% for the Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) and Luminous Red Galaxies (LRG), 95.9% for Emission Line Galaxies (ELG), and 92.6% for quasars (QSO), and it delivers unbiased stellar radial velocities with a precision of roughly 5 km/s.

papers.title: Kinetic theory of dry granular particles under simple shear: steady flows and relaxation dynamics
papers.abstract: We develop a kinetic theory for dry granular particles under simple shear flow using the Enskog approximation combined with Grad's moment method for moderately dense granular gases with the volume fraction $\varphi\le 0.5$. The collisional moments and stresses are expressed in terms of generalized hypergeometric functions, retaining all orders in the dimensionless shear-rate parameter within the adopted Grad closure. Within this framework, we derive a complete set of equations governing the kinetic stress and the collisional contribution to the stress tensor. The steady-state solutions reproduce the shear viscosity over a broad parameter range and improve the predictions of the kinetic temperature relative to the anisotropic Gaussian theory at the parameter values examined. Temperature still shows appreciable deviations under strongly inelastic conditions. Additionally, the theory captures the overall trends of the normal stress differences, while their quantitative accuracy depends on density and restitution coefficient. We further examine relaxation following an instantaneous reduction in $\varphi$ from $0.35$ to $0.20$ at a restitution coefficient of $0.90$. The theory reproduces the temperature and viscosity relaxation for this protocol.

papers.title: Irreducible components of affine Deligne-Lusztig variety in the affine flag variety
papers.abstract: We establish a bijection between elements of stable Demazure crystals and labeled longest increasing paths in the double Bruhat graph. As an application, we show that the orbits of irreducible components of certain special affine Deligne-Lusztig varieties (ADLVs) in the affine flag variety of a split reductive group are counted by weight multiplicities of the associated Demazure modules for the dual group. By decomposing an arbitrary ADLV into strata that are iterated fibrations over these special ADLVs, we then obtain a formula for the number of orbits of irreducible components for ADLVs in the affine flag variety, generalizing the numerical form of the Chen-Zhu conjecture.

papers.title: A higher-order smoothness indicator as refinement criterion for Newtonian and relativistic MHD simulations
papers.abstract: Adaptive mesh refinement is a widely adopted strategy for grid-based numerical simulation codes to mitigate the high computational cost of multi-length scale problems. A robust and reliable mesh refinement criterion with minimal requirement for problem-specific tuning is critical for efficient and accurate simulations. Motivated by the oscillation indicators used in the spectral methods literature, we develop a new mesh refinement criterion employing a 5-point stencil for multi-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations, essentially extending the conventional 3-point Löhner scheme. We implement the criterion in the astrophysical fluid dynamics code AthenaK and test it across a variety of benchmark problems in Newtonian, special relativistic, and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, demonstrating its robustness and versatility.

papers.title: Time-Varying Bayesian Optimization and Extremum Seekingfor Drift-Tube Linac Tuning at LANSCE
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a promising machine learning approach to accelerator tuning. It has the advantage of being able to incorporate prior information, including simulation and historical data, and explicitly model measurement noise. However, standard implementations can produce large, abrupt parameter updates that are undesirable and potentially unsafe in accelerator operation. They may also spend excessive time exploring less promising regions of the search space. We address these limitations by imposing soft and hard step size limits. We evaluate these methods by adjusting the radio frequency settings of the drift tube linac (DTL) at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE) to maximize the particle count at the end of the linac. We first test the methods in simulation with constant exogenous parameters, then repeat the tests with drifting exogenous parameters. Under drifting conditions, progressively reducing the BO step size limit improved convergence. We also find that an initial BO segment followed by extremum seeking (ES), an approach we call BO-ES, combines BO's use of prior information and sample efficiency with ES's effectiveness in local optimization and drift tracking. Finally, tests on the LANSCE accelerator with BO-ES demonstrate an approximately $25\%$ reduction in losses at the end of the linac across different configurations of historical and simulation data.

papers.title: Modeling and Stability of Power Systems With Coupled Data Center and Grid Dynamics
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of data centers poses challenges for power-system operation. However, data centers possess flexible resources that can be leveraged to mitigate their impact on the grid and provide grid services. This paper develops a linear-affine dynamic model of a transmission network with multiple data centers, explicitly coupling electromechanical grid dynamics with data center power demand and computational backlog. Grid-aware computing policies are incorporated to represent how data centers adjust their computational power in response to grid frequency deviations and workload backlog. The proposed framework provides a tractable means of investigating the interactions between multiple data centers and the transmission grid and assessing the potential of flexible computing to support power-system stability.

papers.title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
papers.abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

papers.title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
papers.abstract: Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincaré inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincaré constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

papers.title: Extreme value statistics for majorisation partial orders
papers.abstract: We study extreme-value phenomena for random samples in partially ordered sets through their meets and joins, the order-theoretic analogues of minima and maxima. In this paper we consider the probability simplex equipped with either UT-majorisation or majorisation, with samples drawn uniformly from the corresponding simplex. We analyse these extrema both at fixed dimension and as the dimension grows, identifying almost-sure collapse to the bottom or top elements and critical scalings with nondegenerate limiting laws.

papers.title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
papers.abstract: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy? This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics. While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.

papers.title: Averting `Gravity': Launch Control and the Limits of Collision Avoidance in Low Earth Orbit Operations
papers.abstract: As large constellations fill low Earth orbit, the risk of a runaway collision cascade has become a central concern of space operations. Debris population models treat collision avoidance as a fixed input, although the capacity to screen potential collisions and plan maneuvers degrades as debris accumulates. Using a stylized multi-layer queueing network model, we show that collision avoidance capabilities that saturate as the in-custody fragment count increases, can make the orbital shell bistable, with a low-debris and a high-debris equilibrium, and hysteretic. This has two major operational consequences. First, leaving the high-debris equilibrium requires a large cut in launch rates. Second, in the low-debris equilibrium, fragment counts respond with a delay as the launch rate rises past a tipping point. Removing bistability is desirable, and we show that fragment count-indexed admission control can achieve this. The least restrictive such policy lengthens the lag, whereas an exponential tilt of this policy makes the fragment count track its equilibrium with a bounded lag. Furthermore, admitting more launches can reduce the rate of completed missions, and under a unimodality condition a threshold rule on the debris fragment count maximizes this rate at equilibrium.

papers.title: Persistent Hydration and Ionic Mobility: When the Ion Is Not the Only Transported Species
papers.abstract: Small-ion transport in water remains only partially understood despite more than a century of theoretical work. The difficulty is especially acute for strongly hydrated ions such as Li$^{+}$, Mg$^{2+}$, and Ca$^{2+}$, whose first hydration shells can persist on timescales comparable to or longer than translational motion. We develop a molecular framework in which the ion, its first hydration shell, and the outer solvent are treated as dynamically coupled components. Local hydration structure and exchange are represented through a potential of mean force and coordination dynamics, while collective solvent response is described through molecular memory functions. The theory clarifies why hydration cannot generally be represented by an additive friction or a single enlarged radius, and provides a route beyond conventional continuum and molecular descriptions.

papers.title: Uniformly Convergent Perturbation Theory for Open Quantum Systems at, near, and away from Exceptional Points
papers.abstract: Near a Liouvillian exceptional point, spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned, yet the observable dynamics of a finite-dimensional open system remains regular in the perturbation. Using a Dyson expansion, which requires no diagonalization of the perturbed generator, we analyze the scaling, stability, and convergence of the perturbative corrections at, near and away from exceptional points. We derive scaling laws showing that nonperipheral Jordan blocks raise the degree of the polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials, which are present for any generator as resonances, and we quantify this excess. We further establish a uniform-in-time error estimate for the perturbative series, valid for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian and controlled by a parameter $q = |\varepsilon|R$, where $\varepsilon$ is the perturbation strength and $R$ is a constant built from unperturbed data. All constants of the bound remain continuous through an exceptional point when the coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster. The estimate extends to the frequency domain via the Laplace transform, and to time-dependent perturbations. We test it in a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including perturbations that break its symmetry.

papers.title: Passivity Control for Synchronous Machine Systems using Battery, Field Current and Governor Actuation
papers.abstract: The passivity of synchronous machines enables power system stability to be established from local conditions. A recent state-feedback design enforces robust passivity using battery actuation at the machine terminal bus. This paper extends that design to a model that includes the field winding and the dynamics of a steam turbine and its governor. The extended model provides two additional actuator signals: the exciter input and the governor input. The nonlinear terms in the model depend on speed and field current deviations, and are represented as bounded uncertainties. Robust positive real conditions are derived in terms of a single algebraic Riccati equation. From its solution, a state-feedback controller is designed in closed form. Numerical results show that, unlike the design with battery actuation alone, the proposed controller leads to passivity at all loading levels when the damping is low.

papers.title: Retinal arterial velocity-proxy waveforms from differential spectral broadening in laser Doppler holography
papers.abstract: Laser Doppler holography (LDH) records pulsatile spectral broadening in retinal arteries. We compare vessel and local-background measurements to extract a signed differential-broadening waveform, $\Delta\sigma$. A minimal Gaussian convolution model motivates quadratic subtraction, and Doppler scaling relates the added width to a characteristic blood velocity. Real arteries show pulsatile waveforms, whereas identically processed imaginary arteries show only low-amplitude fluctuations around zero. We interpret the empirically scaled signal as a velocity proxy for waveform shape and within-vessel changes during a single acquisition under stable conditions.

papers.title: Comment on "Exact, nonsingular black holes from a phantom DBI field as primordial dark matter"
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that the metric and scalar configuration proposed in Ref.~[1] do not satisfy the complete set of field equations of the Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) field theory minimally coupled to general relativity on a radial domain containing the event horizon. The physical DBI branch for this gravitational setup terminates outside the event horizon. Thus, the proposed configuration does not describe a black hole solution of that theory.

papers.title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs
papers.abstract: We study variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with feature dimension $d$, horizon $H$, and $K$ episodes. While recent works have established variance-dependent regret with $\tilde{O}(1)$ deterministic-regime overhead for linear mixture MDPs (Zhao et al., 2023) and worst-case nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K} + d^7 H^8)$ for linear MDPs (He et al., 2023),, existing variance-aware analyses for linear MDPs (Li and Sun, 2023; Huang et al., 2023) rely on a coarse concentration step whose resulting regret guarantees retain a polynomial $\tilde{O}(K^{1/4})$ additive term even in deterministic environments. We propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the variance-dependent regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H\min\{\mathrm{Var}_K^*,\mathrm{Var}_K^\pi\}}+d^5H^4)$, where $\mathrm{Var}_K^*$ and $\mathrm{Var}_K^\pi$ denote the cumulative conditional variances of the optimal value function and the played policies' value functions along the realized trajectory. Our result adapts to the minimum of the two realized trajectory variances, recovers the worst-case minimax optimal leading term $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K})$, and collapses to $\tilde{O}(d^5 H^4)$ in deterministic environments, free of polynomial-in-$K$ dependency. At the core of our analysis is a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value function estimators coupled with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments, which tightens the pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by a factor of $\tilde{O}(d H)$ and removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup.

papers.title: Layer-dependent $s^{\pm}$ superconducting pairing and influence of incipient bands in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ thin films on real LaSrAlO$_4$ substrate
papers.abstract: Motivated by recent advances in ambient-pressure superconducting La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ (LNO) thin films, we theoretically investigate these films by explicitly incorporating the realistic LaSrAlO$_4$ (LSAO) substrate. The Fermi-surface topology of the nickelate thin film closely resembles that of the high-pressure bulk phase, with similar $\alpha$ and $\beta$ sheets and a small hole-like $\gamma$ pocket originating from the surface bilayer (BL3). The bonding $d_{3z^2-r^2}$ state of the interfacial bilayer (BL1, adjacent to the LSAO substrate) lies only $\sim 5$ meV below the Fermi level, giving rise to an incipient $\gamma$ band, while for the middle bilayer (BL2) its energy is much lower ($\sim 95$ meV). Remarkably, no significant spontaneous charge transfer from the LSAO substrate to the LNO film is found. Instead, {\it symmetry-allowed charge disproportionation} occurs between the BLs, with hole doping in BL3 and electron doping in BL1 and BL2. Via the weak-coupling Random Phase Approximation, we find a strong $s^{\pm}$-wave superconducting pairing instability in BL3, while $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $s^{\pm}$ are nearly degenerate in the other bilayers BL1 and BL2. Including the incipient $\gamma$ band via the Dynamical Cluster Approximation beyond weak coupling, robust $s^{\pm}$-wave pairing is observed in all three layers

papers.title: Comparison of Open-Source PSCAD EMT Models for Large-Scale AI Data Centers in Smart Grids
papers.abstract: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) introduces gigawatt-scale, highly nonlinear, and fast-varying electronic loads that challenge grid voltage regulation, frequency stability, and disturbance ride-through. Capturing their transient behavior during grid faults and rapid computational workload swings requires high-fidelity electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations rather than root mean square models. However, limited methodologies exist to audit the component-level adequacy of EMT AIDC models. This paper proposes a software-agnostic, 41-point fidelity framework spanning 11 categories that synthesizes 37 criteria from an existing modeling guideline with four novel requirements: frequency ride-through compliance, disaggregated fan and chiller cooling loads, temperature-dependent thermal response, and DC information technology (IT) load representations. Applying this framework to the four publicly available AIDC models in PSCAD/EMTDC reveals varying degrees of completeness: while the models capture IT load transitions, uninterruptible power supplies, and transfer switches for bulk stability studies, critical gaps remain in electro-thermal cooling coupling, internal protective relaying, and site-level controls. Addressing these gaps will enable comprehensive protection coordination and ride-through compliance studies.

papers.title: Cold Magnetized Quark Matter under Compact-Star Conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate the phase structure of cold magnetized two-flavor quark matter under compact-star conditions within a nonlocal chiral quark model with separable interactions. Electric charge neutrality and beta equilibrium are imposed in order to describe matter under realistic neutron-star conditions, while nonlocality is implemented through a Gaussian form factor. We find that low and moderate magnetic fields reduce the critical chemical potential for chiral symmetry restoration, signaling inverse magnetic catalysis. For stronger magnetic fields, the critical chemical potential becomes nearly independent of the magnetic field strength, Compared with the isospin-symmetric case, the combined effects of charge neutrality and beta equilibrium shift the first-order chiral transition to slightly higher chemical potentials, indicating that compact-star constraints delay the onset of chiral symmetry restoration. We further show that charge neutrality and beta equilibrium modify the de Haas--van Alphen oscillations in the quark density, shifting the Landau-level thresholds for the $u$ and $d$ quarks in opposite directions relative to the isospin-symmetric case. The effect on the chiral transition is small ($\sim 5$MeV) for fields $B\lesssim 10^{19}$G, relevant for magnetar interiors, and becomes sizable only for $B\gtrsim 3\times10^{19}$G. These results highlight the importance of incorporating realistic stellar conditions in studies of the QCD phase diagram at high baryon density.

papers.title: Modeling fluid--solid interaction in three-dimensional granular systems: Two-way coupling of SPH and LS-DEM
papers.abstract: This paper presents a two-way coupled fluid--solid interaction framework for granular systems based on the level-set discrete element method (LS-DEM) and smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH). The proposed method is mesh-free, fully Lagrangian, and equipped with a seamless description of arbitrary solid shapes. In particular, a level-set representation of grain geometry is used for both contact detection and fluid--solid coupling, allowing for realistic, highly irregular grains to be handled within a unified computational framework. Moreover, the method incorporates a convenient treatment of moving boundaries and admits a simple computational implementation. The capabilities of the proposed SPH--LS-DEM framework are demonstrated through several numerical benchmarks involving dam-break flow, flow through porous media, granular collapse, and cyclic loading of a saturated granular specimen. The study sets the stage for several extensions to multiphysics problems across disciplines.

papers.title: Perspectives on the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups
papers.abstract: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 $p$-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group $U_4(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$.

papers.title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
papers.abstract: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

papers.title: Spectral Pricing of Corridor Products under Layered Local Volatility
papers.abstract: We price corridor products under a $N$-layered local volatility, piecewise constant in the price and in time, with knock-out barriers. A spatial scale transformation and the GIT method reduce the killed Green's function to a symmetric tridiagonal system of fixed size $N-1$. With equal scaled layer widths the spectrum follows from one tridiagonal eigen-decomposition together with the explicit eigenfunctions that vanish at every interface. For general scaled layer widths an exact counting theorem locates every eigenvalue. Consecutive time intervals of constant volatility are connected by a matrix that re-expands the solution in the eigenbasis of the preceding interval, and the result converges exponentially in the number of retained terms in the eigenfunction expansion. Allowing the killing rate to vary between layers preserves this construction. On a single time interval, the corridor accrual distribution is then recovered by inverting the time and Fourier transforms, without introducing an additional state variable. Exact representations for Greeks and layer vegas follow by differentiation. In our benchmarks the method agrees with independent calculations near rounding error and keeps full accuracy at volatility interfaces, where the tested uniform finite-difference (FD) grids lose one order of convergence. The method computes the accrual law about sixty times faster than the tested FD scheme that includes accrued time as a second state variable.

papers.title: Topological signatures of criticality: the Ising case
papers.abstract: Topological properties of microscopic configurations may provide additional insight into phase transitions beyond conventional thermodynamic observables. We investigate this idea in the two-dimensional Ising model on square and triangular lattices by associating cell complexes with the positive and negative spin domains and constructing an Euler-characteristic observable from their difference. We provide the expression relating this quantity to conventional observables of the Ising model. This derivation allows us to understand its expected behavior physically. As a byproduct, we show that at any finite positive temperature the expectation of the Euler characteristic exceeds a positive, lattice-size-independent bound, hence disproving a previously suggested conjecture. Monte Carlo simulations combined with multihistogram reweighting show that this spin-odd topological observable exhibits order-parameter-like behavior near the ferromagnetic transition. Finite-size scaling of its susceptibility yields pseudocritical temperatures that converge to the known critical temperature for both lattice geometries. On the square lattice, the leading-order estimate of the critical exponent obtained from the topological observable depends more strongly on the fitting range than the magnetization estimate. This behavior is consistent with stronger subleading finite-size corrections, as supported by fits including an additional correction term. On the triangular lattice, the corresponding estimate remains consistent with the theoretical Ising value. Our study suggests that topologically defined quantities such as the Euler characteristic can provide an alternative way to locate order-disorder phase transitions in the systems considered here. Since the definition of these observables is purely geometrical, they can provide useful insights in cases in which order parameters cannot be constructed.

papers.title: SPICE: Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments
papers.abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.

papers.title: The Science and Technology of Broad-Band X-ray Astrophysics
authors: The Broad-Band X-ray Science Analysis Group (BBX-SAG): Chien-Ting Chen (MSFC)
papers.abstract: Much of our understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena over the past decade has relied on coordinated observations extending from soft X-rays (<10 keV) to hard X-rays (>10 keV). While soft X-ray facilities remain abundant, focusing capabilities above ~10 keV are scarce, representing the primary gap for broad-band X-ray science. Simultaneous wide-band observations are essential to study thermal and non-thermal processes in extreme environments such as accretion discs, jets, and coronae. However, current high-energy observations remain limited by a lack of high angular resolution and sensitivity beyond Chandra's bandpass. With upcoming multi-messenger facilities set to dramatically increase variable and transient sources, a high angular resolution broad-band X-ray mission is critically needed. This report reviews the current landscape of high-energy facilities, outlines key science drivers, focusing on extragalactic accretion (the cosmic X-ray background) and Galactic compact objects, and examines the underlying technology landscape, including optics and detectors. Broad-band X-ray astrophysics is primed to address key questions from the Astro2020 Decadal Survey. While past focusing efforts have been limited to the Small Explorer class, technological advances now enable low-risk Probe- or Flagship-class architectures capable of delivering order-of-magnitude improvements in capabilities.

papers.title: Relative periodic orbits of a free spinning loop
papers.abstract: A closed elastic string with no external forces can hold any shape while its material moves steadily along the curve (a steady axial motion), because its tension and the force needed to turn the material around a bend are both proportional to the curvature. I compute the periodic motions that grow from the simplest of these motions, the spinning ring, by Newton's method on a chain of masses. They include rotating waves that turn at twice the rotation rate of the material, standing "flappers" with two to five lobes, and period-doubled and period-tripled orbits. The chain only approximates the string. The orbits and their strong instabilities change little with more masses and are properties of the continuous string. Most weak instabilities change with the number of masses and are artifacts of approximating the string by a finite chain. The saddle flapper of a loop stretched 30% beyond its natural length is neutrally stable at small heights and unstable at large ones. An unstable saddle flapper trades energy back and forth with an in-plane oval, and at large amplitude the energy spreads to the shortest waves of the chain. For Keller's linear string, whose tension is proportional to the stretched length, every motion is periodic, and every knot carries an exactly periodic flapper. For a Hookean string the curvature of a knot couples a ripple to stretching waves that travel at a different speed, and in the simulations a ripple on a sliding knot does not return to its starting shape. Whether a Hookean knot carries any periodic flapper is open.

papers.title: Fuzzy Dark Matter as a diffractive barrier: Wave-optics Signatures of Ultralight Fields on Lensed Gravitational Waves
papers.abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) propagate through the universe from sources at high redshift, experiencing the gravitational fields of the intervening matter distribution. Halos composed of ultralight dark matter (ULDM) contain strong density fluctuations, reflecting the interference pattern in the field distribution of the ultralight bosons. In the wave-optics regime, ULDM fluctuations act as a diffractive grating, imprinting frequency-dependent modulations of GWs, in addition to magnification and other gravitational lensing effects. Since lensing depends on the projected surface density, we derive its approximate probability distribution and show how it departs from a Gaussian distribution depending on the halo profile and coherence length. We then quantify how the GW diffraction signatures produced by the granules depend on macroimage magnification and parity. The ULDM interference network imprints stochastic diffraction fluctuations at the $O(1)\%$ level on GWs moderately lensed by the host when the Fresnel scale is comparable to the granule coherence length $r_F(f)\sim\ell_c$. These fluctuations can be enhanced to $\gtrsim10\%$ when the host macroimage forms near the critical curve or for Type II macroimages. For massive black hole binaries observed by LISA, the diffraction signature can be detectable around the ULDM particle mass $m_\phi\sim10^{-21}$ eV, providing either a smoking-gun signature of ULDM or new constraints on $m_\phi$.

papers.title: Irreducible $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-action on projective $k$-lattices and Frobenius numbers
papers.abstract: The irreducible representation of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ induces an action on the space $X_k(\mathbb{R}^n)$ of projective classes of rank $k$-discrete subgroups in $\mathbb{R}^n$. For every lattice subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ and every starting point in $X_k(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $2\leq k<n$, we prove convergence of the orbit averages over expanding norm balls and give a complete, explicit description of their limits. In an overview, every limit is supported on the subbundle over the unique compact $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-orbit in the Grassmannian. The conditional measures on the fibers are either uniform on finite sets or convex combinations of at most two homogeneous measures associated with split simple subgroups of $\mathrm{PGL}_k(\mathbb{R})$ containing the principal $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$. Another objective of our work is to relate weak-$*$ limits of probability measures on $X_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ supported on the projective classes of lattices orthogonal to integer vectors with limiting distributions of the corresponding normalized Frobenius numbers. This correspondence gives limit laws for vectors sampled from certain proper subvarieties, extending J. Marklof's work on sampling from full-dimensional domains. Specifically, together with our results for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ orbits in $X_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, this correspondence gives limit laws for primitive integer vectors sampled from $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-orbits. Using an earlier result of the first author and Shapira, we obtain analogous laws for integer vectors sampled on level sets of certain quadratic forms, as the level tends to infinity.

papers.title: Perspective on Proton Transversity Distribution Functions
papers.abstract: Using available information on proton tensor charges and constraints from perturbative quantum chromodynamics (QCD), Ansaetze are introduced for hadron-scale in-proton valence-quark transversity distributions functions (DFs). The concept of a QCD effective charge, which defines an evolution scheme for collinear parton distribution and fragmentation functions that is all-orders exact, is then used to deliver predictions for the $x$-dependence of these DFs at the scale $\zeta_{2} = 2\,$GeV. Although the approach is largely algebraic, its predictions remain viable after comparisons with results obtained using computationally intensive methods. Thus, given the scarcity of data that can today be used for inference of proton transversity DFs, it may be worth using the results herein to inform and constrain related experiments and phenomenological fits.

papers.title: Spectral Stability and Convergence of the Unnormalized Graph Laplacian on Noisy Point Clouds
papers.abstract: The first eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the unnormalized graph Laplacian of clean samples from a manifold, suitably scaled, approximate those of a weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator. However, the samples are usually observed with noise and therefore need not lie on the manifold. We build the clean and noisy graph Laplacians, with bandwidth $\varepsilon$, on the clean samples and on the noisy observations, where the noise is arbitrary but bounded by $\delta$. We show that, with high probability, the first eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the noisy graph Laplacian are close to those of the clean one: the eigenvalues within $O(\delta/\varepsilon)$, and the subspaces spanned by the first eigenvectors within $O(\sqrt{\delta/\varepsilon})$, whether or not the eigenvalues are simple. Consequently, if $\delta$ is small enough relative to $\varepsilon$, the noisy graph Laplacian approximates the weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator at the same rate as the clean one. We also show that, for large noise, we can get the same rate as the clean graph Laplacian by first using a denoiser, and then building the graph Laplacian on the denoised observations.

papers.title: ADSPICE: A Method of Automatic Differentiation for Gradient-Based Lumped Circuit Optimization with Native SPICE
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel computer-aided design (CAD) tool for gradient-based circuit optimization using SPICE and automatic differentiation, which we term ADSPICE. Automatic differentiation (AD) is a technique for evaluating a derivative by breaking it into its elementary differentiation operations and repeatedly applying the chain rule, in contrast with a finite-difference-based derivative computed from a small perturbation. Native SPICE (realized with ngspice) is equipped with automatic differentiation toward gradient-based optimization, particularly adjoint-mode optimization. This is implemented with custom C code and shared library control, allowing easy integration with existing SPICE infrastructure. We show a computational performance analysis, demonstrating faster optimization vs. an existing finite-difference method, SPICE OPUS, the closest competitor in SPICE optimization tools. The result is a speedup factor of 383x for the largest circuit compared within the state-of-the-art, SPICE OPUS. For circuit sizes above approximately 3,500 nodes, the time taken by ADSPICE optimization decreases with increasing problem size, as a proportion of total computational time. The speed bottleneck is shown to be SPICE solves rather than ADSPICE enhancements. Voltage gradients needed for forward-mode AD are benchmarked against Xyce, another state-of-the-art simulator, using an integrated CMOS operational amplifier test circuit. The results match with a maximum error of 0.203%, further validating the accuracy of our method. ADSPICE is shown to enable SPICE, and SPICE-based simulators, with automatic differentiation for gradient optimization, without requiring creation of a new circuit simulator.

papers.title: Multiple transition points for an epidemic model
papers.abstract: This paper is concerned with a spatial epidemic model on the $d$-dimensional square lattice that extends the contact process in two ways by assuming that each site is occupied by a social cluster of $N$ individuals rather than a single individual, and that infected individuals can be either asymptomatic or symptomatic. Newly infected individuals begin as asymptomatic and develop the symptoms at a spontaneous mutation rate $\gamma$, and all infected individuals recover at rate one. The model also distinguishes between external (between adjacent clusters) and internal (within clusters) infection rates for each state. Our analysis shows that, when either asymptomatic or symptomatic individuals only spread the disease externally and at a subcritical rate, while the other class only transmits the disease internally and at a large rate, the system exhibits at least two phase transitions with respect to the mutation rate $\gamma$ when social clusters are large. Specifically, the epidemic dies out for extreme values but survives for intermediate values of the mutation rate.

papers.title: Confounding Heterogeneity in Multivariate Sensitivity Analysis for Observational Studies
papers.abstract: In observational studies, unmeasured confounding may bias causal conclusions even after matching on measured confounders. Sensitivity analysis is therefore usually needed to assess the robustness of causal conclusions to unmeasured confounding. We consider multivariate sensitivity analysis that assesses the causal effect of a single treatment on multiple outcomes. We identify an inherent feature of such analyses, which we call ``confounding heterogeneity'': different outcomes may be affected by distinct unmeasured confounders, and a common unmeasured confounder may affect different outcomes to varying degrees. Building on matched observational studies, we formulate sensitivity analysis frameworks that accommodate confounding heterogeneity. We show that Type I error control for many existing sensitivity analysis methods is guaranteed under sensitivity analysis models and modes of inference that differ fundamentally from those used in the classic framework. We study asymptotic power using design sensitivity and Bahadur-Rosenbaum efficiency and examine finite-sample power through numerical studies. Our results show that the structure of unmeasured confounding affects sensitivity analysis, and that widely used single-parameter frameworks may mischaracterize the sensitivity of a causal conclusion to unmeasured confounding when confounding heterogeneity is considered. Simulations and a data application illustrate the practical importance of confounding heterogeneity in multivariate sensitivity analyses.

papers.title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
papers.abstract: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(\rho(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_\rho(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_\rho(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

papers.title: Spatial Extremes on Domains with Physical Barriers
papers.abstract: We propose a model for spatial extremes what realistically accommodates nonconvex domains. Most existing models assume that tail dependence between locations depends only on their separation. Even if extended to be anisotropic or nonstationary, they still cannot accommodate features between points that may mediate the dependence. This assumption limits their applicability in settings where physical barriers like mountains, coastlines, or islands may attenuate or even block dependence in extreme events. In this work, we use the idea of a visibility graph to modify an existing spatial random scale model. This results in a tail dependence model that naturally accommodates nonconvex spatial domains, where the nonconvex features are interpreted as physical barriers. Furthermore, the model inherits key properties from the scale mixture like the ability to represent asymptotic independence at long ranges and either asymptotic dependence or asymptotic independence at short ranges. We apply our model to two applications in which physical barriers feature prominently in determining the spatial structure of extreme events. The first is precipitation in the South Island of New Zealand, where the Southern Alps shelter the eastern region from the effects of atmospheric rivers which arrive from the west. The second is significant wave heights in the North Atlantic, where the Faroe Islands tend to block the effects of extratropical cyclones traveling into the North Sea.

papers.title: Machine-learned acceleration of earthquake sequence simulations
papers.abstract: Earthquake sequence simulations involve slow interseismic processes and rapid dynamic ruptures. During interseismic periods, a numerical solver can take large time steps efficiently. During seismic periods, in contrast, the solver must drastically reduce the time step, and elastodynamic wave-mediated memory effects become significant; long-term simulations are therefore computationally expensive. We investigate the use of neural operators to accelerate earthquake sequence simulations. We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) on data from high-fidelity, fully dynamic simulations to learn a jump map that advances the system state from before a seismic rupture to after it. We propose a hybrid modeling framework in which a conventional quasi-dynamic solver simulates the slow interseismic evolution, and the trained FNO replaces the solver during the computationally intensive seismic periods with wave-mediated inertial effects. The hybrid model reproduces key long-term statistics of fully dynamic simulations, including distributions of event magnitudes and recurrence times. Furthermore, it provides a much better approximation to the fully dynamic simulations than the commonly used quasi-dynamic approximation at a reduced computational expense.

papers.title: 3-Cube-Free Sets in Cyclic Groups
papers.abstract: A set is called $3$-cube-free if it contains no configuration of the following form: $\{x,y,z,x+y,x+z,y+z,x+y+z\}$. We study the maximum density of $3$-cube-free sets in finite cyclic groups. As observed by Meng, every $3$-cube-free subset of $\mathbb Z_m$ has size at most $2m/3$, and this bound is sharp whenever $3\mid m$. Our main result shows that there exists an absolute constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that, for every $m$ not divisible by $3$, every $3$-cube-free subset of $\mathbb{Z}_m$ has size at most $\left(2/3-\varepsilon\right)m$. Thus, in this setting, the natural $2/3$ barrier can be uniformly improved. Long and Wagner conjectured that every $3$-cube-free subset of $\mathbb Z_{2^n}$ has size at most $5\cdot 2^n/8$. We also establish this conjecture for 3-cube-free sets whose density in the layer of odd residues is at least $2/3$. Together with induction, this reduces the conjecture to the case where this density lies in $(5/8,2/3)$.

papers.title: Spectral Disks for Quantum Markov Generators
papers.abstract: Spectral bounds for Markov generators require a choice of time scale. In quantum dynamics, a rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state and the smallest spectral disk need not agree. We prove that the spectrum of every GKLS generator written without a Hamiltonian lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis, with radius given by the norm of the operator $\Phi^\dagger(I)$ built from the jump map $\Phi$. This settles the first two scaling conjectures of "Corralling spectra of generators of time-continuous Markov evolution (both classical and quantum)", J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {59}, 175202 (2026). The third, escape-rate conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Nevertheless, twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup For GKLS generators with vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always supplies a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension. We compare these bounds with classical Cassini ovals and thermodynamic ellipses, explain the obstacles to their quantum extensions, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.

papers.title: Deep-Learning-Assisted Full Waveform Inversion for Attenuation Reconstruction in Ultrasound Computed Tomography
papers.abstract: Acoustic attenuation is more challenging to reconstruct and has received less attention than sound speed in ultrasound computed tomography using full-waveform inversion (FWI). In this study, a deep-learning (DL)-assisted FWI framework was proposed for attenuation reconstruction based on our previous work. Some numerical experiments were conducted to investigate the strategy and the effectiveness of using DL to help accelerate and improve the reconstruction quality of attenuation imaging in FWI. The results indicated that DL saved computational cost by 28% and improved attenuation reconstruction accuracy by 70% when combined with sufficiently accurate sound speed estimates. The result supports the potential of DL initialization to improve the computational efficiency and reconstruction quality of joint SOS and attenuation FWI.

papers.title: Beyond RSRP: An Exploration of Alternative Metrics for Beam Management in an Urban Micro 5G NR Scenario
authors: Daniel J. Jakubisin (2) ((1) Wireless @ Virginia Tech
(2) Hume Center for National Security and Technology
